research_question: How can a best‑possible‑world theological argument be reformulated to include non‑hedonic goods such as authentic relationships, agency, and achievement while still grounding the overall value ranking in divine appreciation of mathematical elegance?

argument.title: Best‑Possible‑World Theodicy
argument.paper_title: A Theological Argument for an Everett Multiverse

premises.text: The actual world is the best possible world.
premises.quote: The actual world is the best possible world.

premises.text: Total goodness of the world is the intrinsic value—pleasure minus suffering—of all conscious experiences.
premises.quote: But when I consider the total goodness of the world, I do mean intrinsic value—pleasure minus suffering, happiness minus unhappiness, joy minus agony—of all conscious experiences that occur.

premises.text: Our universe contains both happiness and suffering, so its intrinsic happiness alone is unlikely to be maximal.
premises.quote: Now I have personally experienced a lot of happiness in my life, and I have seen many other people appear to be happy, so I do think that our universe does have considerable positive intrinsic value. But there is also much suffering and unhappiness, so it does not seem very plausible that the intrinsic happiness within this universe alone is the maximum logically possible.

premises.text: The universe’s high mathematical elegance adds to its intrinsic value.
premises.quote: However, besides the mixed happiness that our universe contains, our universe seems to have a very high degree of mathematical elegance and beauty. Humans can partially appreciate some of this elegance, so it does seem to increase the intrinsic value of the universe.

premises.text: A Being outside the universe could have enormous appreciation for its mathematical elegance.
premises.quote: But if one considers the possibility that there may be a Being outside the universe that has an enormous appreciation for the mathematical elegance of the universe, and perhaps an even greater appreciation if that Being were the Creator of the universe, then it seems that the hypothesis that the actual world is the best possible world might plausibly lead to what I call the Optimal Argument for the Existence of God as such a Being outside the universe who created and experiences tremendous value in having much greater knowledge and appreciation for the mathematical elegance of the universe than we creatures within the universe can have.

premises.text: The best‑possible‑world hypothesis fits better with a world containing an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God than with a world where the universe stands alone.
premises.quote: The hypothesis that the actual world is the best possible world certainly appears to me to be more consistent with a world with an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent Being (which I shall henceforth call God, since these are the main properties traditionally assigned to God), than with a world in which our universe stands alone, with its mathematical elegance not fully appreciated.

missing_premise.text: If the actual world is the best possible world, then an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God exists who creates and values a mathematically elegant universe.

conclusion.text: From the best‑possible‑world hypothesis it follows that an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God exists who creates and values a mathematically elegant universe.

challenged_premise.text: Total goodness of the world is the intrinsic value—pleasure minus suffering—of all conscious experiences.

objection: World A contains one hundred humans wired to a flawless pleasure machine. Every moment is engineered delight; no suffering exists; their pleasure-minus-suffering score is one million. World B contains one hundred humans living real lives: they love, raise children, discover truths, and create art, but they also feel grief, cold, and failure, yielding a score of five hundred thousand. Everyone who grasps both worlds prefers B. The inhabitants of B would refuse to enter A even if promised tripled pleasure, because they value authentic connection and real accomplishment over raw feeling. Since World B is genuinely better despite a lower pleasure-minus-suffering total, total goodness cannot be identical to that sum.

strongest_responses.response: You are right that c008, read as a complete account of total goodness, is vulnerable to your Worlds A and B. ... The honest repair is to read c008 as a partial or hedonic component of value, not as the whole of it. ... Once total value includes authenticity, achievement and relations, the argument owes an account of how the divine appreciation in c011 bears on those goods, and c010's appeal to elegance does not by itself settle which goods count.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: Even after revising c008 to a partial component, the defender does not explain how divine appreciation of mathematical elegance (c011) translates into value for non‑hedonic goods, leaving the link between God’s appreciation and creaturely authenticity unaccounted for.

strongest_responses.response: You are right that World B is better than World A, and your thought experiment lands against c008 as a complete theory of value. ... Because of this, the argument can absorb your point: the inhabitants of B value authentic connection and accomplishment because these are genuine intrinsic goods that a pleasure machine cannot replicate. ... The argument needs to broaden its measure of creaturely value to include the satisfactions of real agency, love, and discovery alongside pleasure and suffering, while keeping the later appeal to divine appreciation of mathematical elegance.
strongest_responses.why_it_failed: The revision broadens the value measure but still offers no principled justification for why divine appreciation of elegance should outweigh or complement these added non‑hedonic goods, so the argument’s explanatory power remains incomplete.

nearest.title: Well-Being and Death * By BEN BRADLEY
Divine Perfection, Axiology and the No Best World Defence

open_questions: What formal framework can aggregate hedonic and non‑hedonic values into a single total‑goodness metric suitable for a best‑possible‑world claim?
How does divine appreciation of mathematical elegance interact with, or possibly rank among, creaturely goods such as authentic relationships and achievement?
In an Everett multiverse, how should values be summed across branches, and does this affect the assessment of the actual world’s maximality?
Can the revised premise be defended without invoking contentious meta‑ethical assumptions about the intrinsic status of non‑hedonic goods?
paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the theological best‑possible‑world argument can be salvaged by constructing a composite axiological account that treats hedonic balance, authentic agency, relational depth, and artistic achievement as co‑intrinsic goods, and then shows how a divine appreciation of mathematical elegance provides a supervenient, non‑exhaustive source of additional value. The case would begin by formalizing a pluralistic value function, demonstrate that Worlds A and B illustrate the insufficiency of a pure pleasure‑minus‑suffering metric, and then integrate the divine aesthetic appreciation as a weighting factor that does not eclipse but complements creaturely goods. Anticipating Defender A’s concern, the paper would develop a principled account—perhaps via a divine‑valuational hierarchy or a relational‑aesthetic synthesis—explaining how God’s appreciation of elegance translates into increased worth for authenticity and achievement. To succeed, the paper must show that this enriched metric still permits the claim that the actual Everett‑multiverse world maximizes total goodness, and that the added complexity does not undermine the argument’s explanatory coherence.

reasons.coherence: The objection is a recognisable experience-machine case and is aimed squarely at c008, but the proposal is muddled: it calls divine appreciation 'supervenient' and a 'weighting factor' that raises the worth of creaturely goods without saying what that means, and it never notices that c008's hedonism is what makes divine appreciation count as a conscious-experience good.
reasons.robustness: Neither the direction nor the transcript addresses the obvious reply that pluralism removes the reason for invoking God's appreciation, and the 'divine-valuational hierarchy' is offered only as a 'perhaps'.
reasons.significance: Even if it succeeded, it would mainly re-apply Nozick to one niche argument; the argument's weakest point, the unsupported move from 'best world' to 'God exists' (the bridging premise), goes untouched.
reasons.specificity: There is a stated thesis and a rough sequence of steps, but the central mechanism is not specified, and the Everett branch-aggregation question is listed as open even though the argument's conclusion depends on it.

assessment.strongest_objection: The proposed repair defeats the argument it is meant to save. In the original argument, c008's hedonism does real work: because value is pleasure minus suffering, a universe with suffering cannot be maximal on its own (c009), so the missing value is supplied by a divine conscious appreciation of elegance (c010–c011). God's appreciation is itself a conscious experience, which is why hedonism suits it. Once authenticity, agency and achievement count as intrinsic goods, creaturely suffering can be offset by those goods in soul-making fashion, so the inference from 'suffering exists' to 'extra value must come from God's appreciation' loses its motivation. The paper's remaining task, showing how God's appreciation of elegance 'translates into increased worth for authenticity and achievement', is also an unexplained mechanism. Separately, the experience-machine case simply stipulates that World B is better, which a hedonist will deny with familiar replies (status-quo bias, De Brigard's reversed machine).
assessment.what_it_needs: The paper must show why, on a pluralist axiology, divine appreciation of elegance is still needed to make the actual world best. Without that, c009–c011 become idle. It must also engage the hedonist replies to Nozick's experience machine and the existing best-world literature (Rowe, Kraay, Page) instead of assuming World B's superiority.
assessment.summary: A familiar objection attached to a repair plan that, if carried out, would remove the reason the argument appeals to God at all; not yet a defensible paper.

revision.research_question: On a hedonist axiology, can a divine conscious appreciation of mathematical elegance be the supplement that makes the actual world best, and can the experience-machine objection be answered without assuming that World B is better?
revision.paper_direction: A paper here would argue that the best-possible-world argument cannot keep its divine-appreciation step if value is pluralised, and that it survives only in a narrower form that keeps hedonism (c008) as its axiological base. The paper would first set out a dilemma. If authenticity, agency and achievement are intrinsic goods, creaturely goods can offset suffering in a soul-making pattern, so the inference from suffering to a deficit that only God's appreciation of elegance can fill (c009-c011) loses its motivation. If value is hedonic, the deficit inference holds, but the Worlds A and B case must be met on its merits. The paper would take the second horn. It would defend hedonism against the experience-machine case by engaging the status-quo bias reply and the reversed-machine reply (De Brigard) rather than assuming World B's superiority. It would then specify the mechanism that c008 requires: divine appreciation counts as a good only because it is a conscious experience, so it contributes to the hedonic total without any further account of how elegance raises the worth of other goods. The paper would drop the claim that divine appreciation translates into increased worth for authenticity and achievement. It would then treat the bridging premise from best world to God's existence as a separate section, since that premise is the argument's weakest point. The Everett branch-aggregation question would be stated as a dependency that the conclusion relies on and that this paper does not settle. The paper would position the narrowed argument against the best-world literature (Rowe, Kraay, Page) without claiming to refute or extend it.
revision.reply_to_strongest_objection: The paper accepts the referee's dilemma and does not adopt pluralism for the divine step. Under pluralism c009-c011 become idle, so the paper keeps c008. It answers the experience-machine case with two specific replies: the status-quo bias reply, which says the preference for B may track a default rather than value, and the reversed-machine reply, which asks whether a hedonist should prefer an experience machine that is reversed to deliver suffering-free misery in the same way. The paper argues that the hedonist must accept that its verdicts on these cases are the cost of the view, and states that cost openly. It drops the unexplained mechanism of 'increased worth' and replaces it with the hedonic account: divine appreciation is a conscious-experience good and so counts in the total. The bridging premise is addressed separately, not assumed.
revision.what_changed: The revision narrows the thesis to a hedonist version in which divine appreciation is a conscious-experience good, drops the pluralist weighting mechanism, and treats the bridging premise and Everett aggregation as explicit dependencies.

reasons.coherence: The direction targets c008 as actually stated and frames the dilemma well, but it asserts rather than shows that pluralism makes c009-c011 idle, and it misdescribes the reversed-machine reply ('suffering-free misery' is not De Brigard's case).
reasons.robustness: The plan says the hedonist should state its costs openly, but it never addresses the central difficulty for its own key move: whether God's pleasure belongs in the world's total at all, and if so, how it avoids swamping, idleness, or circularity.
reasons.significance: Defending hedonism against the experience machine with status-quo-bias replies is well-trodden ground, and narrowing an idiosyncratic argument would be a modest refinement rather than something that changes the best-world debate.
reasons.specificity: There is a definite thesis (keep hedonism, narrow the divine step), a stated dilemma, named replies, and a section structure, though the crucial hedonic-aggregation mechanism gets only a single sentence.

assessment.strongest_objection: Treating divine appreciation as a hedonic good in the world's total either trivialises the argument or undermines it. If God's appreciative pleasure belongs to the actual world's value, an unbounded divine term swamps all creaturely suffering, so c009 does no work and 'best world' becomes a claim about God's experience rather than about the universe. If, as most theists hold, God's beatitude is already maximal and unaffected by creation, the term adds nothing to any created world and cannot fill the deficit. On either reading the inference from best world to God is circular, because the world counts as best only if God's experience is already in the total.
assessment.what_it_needs: The paper must show that a divine hedonic term can enter the world's total without swamping it, without being idle given divine impassibility or beatitude, and without presupposing God's existence in the best-world premise. It must also give a correct version of De Brigard's reversed-machine case and argue for the first horn of the dilemma, that pluralism makes c009-c011 idle, rather than asserting it.
assessment.summary: This is a tidy, well-organised plan, but its central move of counting God's pleasure in the hedonic total invites an obvious swamping-or-circularity objection that the proposal never confronts, so it is not yet a defensible paper.
